items.title: They don't make 'em like that any more: Borland Turbo Pascal 7
items.author: andsoitis
items.content:
Borland’s was one of the most successful programming tools of all time. It introduced development techniques, such as integrated source-level debugging, that we take for granted today; but which were radical at the time.

TP 7, also known as Turbo Pascal for Windows 1.5, was the pinnacle of the Turbo Pascal line, and its end. The name ‘Turbo’ was associated with what were regarded as hobbyist products – ‘Borland Pascal’ was a different, much more expensive, product. But Turbo Pascal was enough for some quite substantial applications, and was very affordable. It was also ‘book licensed’, which I think was a new thing in the software industry. You could buy one copy of TP, and any number of people could use it – but only one at a time. Even when it was distributed on floppy disks, there was no copy protection. (Turbo) Pascal eventually gave way to Delphi which, despite its technical merits, never had the same impact.

I used TP 7 to write medical imaging software back in the 90s, to run under Windows 3.1 – which was a great operating system in its day. Like previous releases, Windows 3.1 was still, essentially, an extension to MSDOS, but with clever tricks to allow it to multitask (after a fashion) and address more memory. It had a simple, consistent user interface model – both for the user and the programmer. It had, at that time, none of the wasteful and irritating anti-features that have come to make modern Windows so depressing to use. So Windows 3.1 was a platform we all wanted our applications to support – not that there were many alternatives at that time.

Like many other programmers, I learned the Pascal programming language specifically to use TP 7 – I was essentially a C programmer in those days, but programming for Windows in C was a horrible job. Frankly, it’s scarcely better today. It was, and is, necessary to combine a whole stack of command-line tools that take incomprehensible text files as input. TP 7 automated and concealed all that nastiness.

It wasn’t just the tools that were a problem: the user interface model was, essentially, object-oriented; but C did not make it easy to program in an object-oriented way. TP 5 had introduced basic object-oriented concepts to the Pascal language, and these were were to prove essential. The Windows-specific features were provided by something called : a relatively thick, object-oriented wrapper around the basic Windows C API. My recollection is that Borland introduced an object-oriented programming library for Microsoft Windows before Microsoft did – and Borland’s was better.

OWL made it easy to create nice-looking user interfaces, with a bit of eye candy. The familiar ‘green tick button’ was an OWL enhancement, which graced so many Windows applications that it eventually became an irritating cliche.

All, in all, It was easier to program for Windows using Turbo Pascal 7 than with anything else. Not only did it provide a programming model that matched the way the Windows user interface worked, the application itself had a Windows graphical interface – many Windows programming tools at that time actually ran under MSDOS, and were entirely text-based. TP 7 also had fully-graphical tools for designing the user interface elements, like menus and icons. Laying out a menu using a definition file with an obscure format, using Windows Notepad, was never an agreeable experience. Microsoft did produce graphical tools for this kind of operation, but Turbo Pascal combined them into a seamless IDE. All I had to do to build and run my programs was to hit the F7 key. I could even set breakpoints for the debugger, just by clicking a line of code. As I said, common enough today, but revolutionary for early Windows programming.

But what really made TP 7 special was its CP/M heritage. Turbo Pascal came to Windows by way of CP/M and MSDOS, which meant it had a compiler core that was designed to run with tight memory and a comparatively slow CPU. In the days when most compilers had to write a stack of intermediate files on disk, TP just constructed everything in memory. It did this using highly-optimized code, written in assembly language, by very skilled people. It doesn’t matter much today if your compiler spits out a heap of temporary files, because disk storage is fast and cheap. But in the days of the floppy disk, you had to minimize disk access. Unfortunately, you had to minimize memory use, because there wasn’t much of that, either. Programming for CP/M took real skill and dedication.

So when TP came to Windows machines, with their 16-bit CPUs and megabytes of RAM, it was like an early Christmas for developers. A compiler designed to be adequate with 32kB of RAM and a single floppy drive will positively fly when given megabytes and a hard disk.

All this meant that TP 7 was a joy to use. It was like a modern IDE, but without any of the bloat. Developers who would never have tackled Windows programming with Microsoft tools were able to move from MSDOS to Windows without too much difficulty – even if they first had to learn Pascal, as I did. The compiled code was pretty speedy but, if it wasn’t brisk enough, you could write assembly language directly in the Pascal source files.

I don’t think it’s too much of an exaggeration to claim that Turbo Pascal contributed to the widespread uptake, and eventual domination, of Microsoft Windows on desktop PCs. If there had been a ‘Turbo Pascal for Linux’ in the early 90s, then we might be running Linux on our desktops today.

So what happened to Turbo Pascal? Three things, at least, contributed to its eventual downfall.

First, there was increasing competition from the C programming language. Borland did produce a Turbo C, and later a Turbo C++, but they weren’t as influential as Pascal. It’s easy to forget that PCs weren’t the first general-purpose computing devices. Most scientific and educational establishments, and many businesses, used graphical workstations and a central minicomputer. C was already well-established in these environments before desktop computers started to become prominent. And before that we had mainframes and terminals – but that was a different world, where Fortran and COBOL ruled.

Most ‘serious’ PC applications were written in assembly language in the early days, as they had been for CP/M – the low resources almost necessitated this. Minicomputers were not so limited, so compilers were more practicable, even in the 1980s. So when compilers started to become of interest to microcomputer developers, there was almost no reason to favour one programming language over another. Pascal have become the standard programming language for the PC. That it did not, I think, reflects the fact that many software companies that had been active in industrial and scientific computing saw an opportunity in PCs, and tried to move into that market. These companies already had substantial experience with C, and they brought their preferences with them. So while I was happy to learn a new programming language to develop for Windows, a software business with a thousand staff might not have wanted to take that step.

The second factor, I think, was the increasing palatability of Microsoft’s C tools. Microsoft did eventually produce an IDE of its own and, of course, Microsoft controlled the Windows platform. I don’t think Microsoft’s C IDEs became as easy to use as Borland’s, but they probably didn’t have to, given Microsoft’s position.

Third, Microsoft’s Visual BASIC started to attact small-scale and bespoke developers. BASIC was already a staple of the microcomputing world, because it was easy to learn, and did not require a separate compilation step. Attaching bits of BASIC code to Windows user interface elements was an efficient way to produce relatively simple, small-volume applications.

I loathed Visual BASIC in the 90s, and I loathed it until the day VB6 drew its last laboured, wheezing breath in 2005. Still, I can’t deny its popularity, and I’m sure that many of the same people who were drawn to Turbo Pascal were later drawn to Visual BASIC, for much the same reasons. VB lowered the barriers to entry into Windows programming in the same way that TP had previously done. Arguably it lowered them too much, but let’s not go there today.

Early versions of Turbo Pascal are now freely, and legally, available. Retrocomputing enthusiasts with an interest in early PCs and MSDOS are well catered for. So far as I know, however, TP 7 remains somebody’s intellectual property, although it isn’t entirely clear whose. It probably comes into the category of ‘abandonware’ but, to be frank, it’s not all that important: it can’t produce code that runs on modern Windows systems, and few people have much interest in early Windows – it’s just not retro enough.

So that’s Turbo Pascal: a colossus of the microcomputing world, which faded and died largely unlamented. It always was a creature of its time – it prospered for the brief period when microcomputers were limited enough to reward skilled development, but widespread enough to create a substantial market for programmers. By the time it started to become difficult to find enough highly-skilled programmers to satisfy the market needs, it didn’t matter: computers were getting powerful enough to make good our limitations as programmers. That almost nobody has the skills these days to implement something like TP is something we could eventually come to regret – or, rather, our grandchildren could. Software development is becoming a semi-skilled industry, and I doubt that the rise of AI will entirely compensate for this.

But who needs a Turbo Pascal, when you have 128Gb of RAM attached to an 5GHz CPU, for a hastily-written, bloated Java program to burn?

items.title: Running a law firm on Free software
items.author: DeepLogin
items.content:
I started running decoded.legal - a small English law firm, focussing on Internet, telecoms, and tech law - on Free software, both client and server side, around five years ago. I have used Free software in my personal life for a lot longer than that.

Someone asked me recently what I am doing now, and, while it is mostly the same, some bits have changed. So here is the 2026 update.

I am still using Debian, with GNOME, and it works well for me.

However, the machine itself seems to have a hardware problem with the Thunderbolt / USB-C ports (fine for power, very flaky for data), and so I might need to replace it. And I have idea what laptop I might get.

  • Email (MUA): and , depending on what I am doing

    • Quick Folder Move and Move Message And Yourself are particularly useful add-ons for Thunderbird, for rapid filing of email with keyboard shortcuts
    • Thunderbird seems to be having a problem with some recurring calendar invitations, while is handling them fine. I’ve not dug into it, but it is a nuisance.

  • PDFs: for most reading; for marking up PDFs; and for interfering with PDFs

    • This is a fantastic shortcut for me, saving me from typing the same thing multiple times. I have loads of shortcuts set up, and I’d be lost without them.
    • I am still using Firefox. It is … fine? I should probably look at LibreWolf or another fork, as I’m not enamoured by Mozilla’s direction of travel but, for now, Firefox it is.
    • I use Firefox for joining people’s Teams and Zoom etc. meetings, if someone else sets up the meeting, and that works fine

  • Local wiki / knowledge management:

    • because I use vim so much, was quite an obvious choice.
    • I use this for keeping track of my professional development, and for various notes

  • Client-side encryption of files before syncing them with :

  • Fediverse: I tend to use the advanced web UI or, when I want fewer images, the TUI .

  • Password manager: , using the server, with YubiKeys for managing more sensitive credentials

  • Markdown editor (for blogposts; I do presentations in vim or gedit):

Why so many terminal-based tools? The simple answer is that I am very comfortable in a terminal, and I like them. They have fewer distractions and, when compared with most GUI software, are just - IMHO - easier to use, especially when I don’t need to move my hands away from the keyboard. So, while I don’t use them exclusively, I use , , , , , , , and various other TUIs, frequently.

Everything here - other than Signal - is self-hosted, and I’m mostly using Intel NUCs now. I still have some Raspberry Pi devices, but fewer than I did.

(Again, this doesn’t list everything; just the main applications.)

  • Email (MTA):

    • I need to move our mail infrastructure at some point, and I want to look at Stalwart.

  • File synchronisation:

    • One of the bigger changes since last time was moving away from Nextcloud. I just was not getting on with it, and it was causing me more problems than it solved. So I switched to Syncthing for file sync, and radicale for CalDAV / CardDAV. I’ve been more than happy with this combination.

  • Video conferencing:

    • I ran jitsi for years, but stopped using it a few months back. Jitsi is great, and I remain a fan, but most of the time I am joining other people’s Teams or Zoom meetings, so I was running the Jitsi server for very little usage. I turned it off, and instead offer Signal. I have had no grumbles.

  • Invoicing and tracking payments: , just for generating PDF invoices. Clients don’t interact with it

    • v2 of Kimai is excellent, and I had a very pleasant exchange with the developer, which is always nice.

  • “Case management” / “Matter management”:

  • VPN: , using trailofbit’s ansible scripts on one machine, and on another (albeit not on a Pi)

  • Vulnerability scanning:

    • I implemented this not long after the last update. It … just works?

  • Forge / hosted git repository:

    • I use this for version tracking the website, and for a couple of template projects
    • I do not host anything particularly important on it - for that, I have a git process running on another machine, which is not accessible over the Internet, and I just push to that

  • Password manager:

  • Website: it is a static site built via , hosted on

    • It got even simpler and even faster to load. Yes, it’s basic, but I like it!
    • After a couple of annoyances with hugo, I moved to BSSG - a bash static site generator. The developer, Stefano, is amazing, and it is working incredibly well. I’ve gone for a very basic, easy to read, theme - which should be very similar to what was there before - and there’s still an RSS feed for it, of course
    • I blog quite frequently, and, rather than keep private / internal “knowhow” files, I tend to just blog things and share the learnings
    • I have automated the most common actions - templates, and publishing - using bash scripts, so that I can focus on writing (in Markdown); getting it online is the easiest bit

  • Fediverse: I am using the *glitch-soc Mastodon** fork

    • I stopped using Markdown in toots, even though I like the rendered output (i.e. as html not as markdown), but this is not supported consistently well across clients, so I stopped using it.
    • I turned off decoded.legal’s own fedi instance. I had been on the fence as to whether this is worthwhile or not for a while, and decided that, really, it was not.

  • Knowledge management, and managing our law firm’s (numerous) policies and procedures: with the Markdown plugin

  • DNS: , with in front of it

    • I used to run a doh server, but I’ve stopped doing that.
    • I have been really happy with LiberaForms, for easy-to-create and easy-to-use forms, especially since they implemented encryption, so that the form responses are stored encrypted on the server. I still delete them as soon as I can, but knowing that they are encrypted in the database is welcome.
    • I use LiberaForms for our “Know Your Client” pre-engagement questionnaire, and for various other bits

  • Collaborative document editing: I don’t.

    • I used to run CryptPad, but it just didn’t get much use, so I turned it off.

I’m using a Pixel running GrapheneOS for my mobile device.

I use F-Droid as the main app store.

Using Android doesn’t thrill me, especially given Google’s direction of travel, but at the moment - despite trying quite a lot of different OSs and devices, including postmarketOS and Ubuntu Touch, as well as SailfishOS previously - I have not found something that does what I need better than GrapheneOS.

No change here: zero problems.

Many of my clients use Microsoft’s software, or Apple’s software.

items.title: The Components of Agent Memory
items.author: geoffbp
items.content:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood , but it must be lived . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.

As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge.

Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest, the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.

Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called (Figure 1).

We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.

By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their (the internal parameters set during training), (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).

In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.

Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?

Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need

Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.

Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0, a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.

Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.

We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using Claude Managed Agents. Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next.

Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.

Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.

Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).

Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.

Claude has learned to judge salience

We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play , a game that challenges Claude to navigate complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).

We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).

Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called , and earned four badges.

Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.

Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.

Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”

With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.

Steering Claude to write memory

We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).

We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.

We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.

In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.

With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.

Dreaming can correct memory

Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.

Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.

In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.

At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.

We then tested whether dreaming could help Claude avoid this trap. We ran dreaming on the memory folder that contained the wrong location for the PokéCenter: Claude checked the note against the session transcript, caught its error, and rewrote it. The transcript gave Claude a ground truth to validate its memory against. With the corrected memory note, Claude went straight back into Mt. Moon and eventually reached Cerulean City.

In the run with the uncorrected note, Claude dropped back onto that earlier route three times. After the third failure, Claude seemed to give up, writing, “I’m going to stop rather than keep looping.” Our setup’s automatic reply instructed it to continue. So it did, all the way back to Pewter City, the town before the mountain, where it hoped to heal and restock. The run ended without Claude ever reaching Cerulean City.

Dreaming can build new memory representations

With dreaming, Claude can build representations to help navigate memory (Figure 9). One type of memory representation it uses is called a , a collection of pages written and maintained by Claude that gathers what Claude knows about one subject and links it to other notes. These links effectively provide Claude with a map it can use to sift through its memory and efficiently locate memories when they’re needed.

Representations like wikis can help Claude traverse its ever-growing knowledge base. We explored the benefit of wikis as a memory representation using a corpus of internal documents—about 350,000 files, roughly 420M tokens—from Stainless, a software company we acquired in May. We created an evaluation set of 25 questions about this corpus and gave Claude a search tool to explore it. We also instructed Claude to build a wiki based on these files using dreaming. Over 128 sessions, we prompted Opus 5 agents to explore the files, write or correct linked wiki pages, merge duplicates, and check claims against the sources.

Each session built on the progress that agents made in prior sessions, using a shared log to coordinate work. As we scaled dreaming from two sessions to 128, performance on the 25 questions grew from 13% to 48% of graded criteria (Figure 10).

Claude builds its wikis incrementally. After creating an initial wiki, it uses subsequent rounds of dreaming to add to, edit, or prune it. In the early rounds of dreaming, Claude’s knowledge is like that of a new employee, and its ability to answer questions based on the wiki alone is limited. The more it dreams, the richer its knowledge map grows, like that of a seasoned employee. In our tests, we found that the wiki helped Claude the most when we also gave it access to a search tool. When it used both search and the wiki, Claude’s aggregate score rose from 54% to 61% as that wiki grew, compared with 53% when it had access to the search tool alone. Claude’s best score was 48% when it used only the wiki to answer questions. Using search and the wiki also saved about 20,000 tokens per question.

We wanted to test which kinds of tasks benefited from Claude having a wiki. To do this, we used the Harvey LAB benchmark along with a collection of documents about a merger. The benchmark gives Claude a set of documents and asks Claude to generate a legal brief based on their content. The benchmark then grades the brief against a list of criteria. While a tad less engaging, perhaps, than a Pokémon run, these evaluations give us diverse collections of documents to build wikis from.

We instructed Claude to build a wiki from the documents. We then asked Claude to answer questions (about the merger) or generate legal briefs (the LAB benchmark) both from the wiki and from a direct file search. One test asked 24 questions about the merger (Figure 11, left), more than half of which needed Claude to find information across several documents, and many of which also needed Claude to use judgment or do math. On those items (red and orange lines), Claude scored 87% when it consulted the wiki, compared with 73% when it used search alone.

In other cases, the wiki was less useful. On one LAB task (Figure 11, right), brief criteria often could be retrieved with a text search from a single document, and the wiki showed no clear gain in performance relative to search. On another LAB task, the wiki grew larger than the documents themselves (Figure 12). Like the mapmakers in Borges’s one-paragraph short story “On Exactitude in Science,” who drafted a map so detailed it was as large as the empire it represented, Claude had made an extremely detailed wiki that effectively abstracted nothing.

Dreaming can promote notes up the memory hierarchy

Dreaming can also float notes to the top of the memory hierarchy, and the agent harness can preemptively load them into Claude’s context at the start of every session (Figure 13). This means Claude doesn’t need to search for them, or even to know there’s something to search for.

Promoting memories into a new session (a form of ) must be done carefully. Injected memories use up valuable tokens, and an incorrect note can be carried into every session. Loading a note also doesn’t guarantee that Claude acts on it: our documentation on Claude Code warns that longer instruction files reduce adherence. So the top layer of the memory hierarchy has to stay relatively small, and much of dreaming’s work here is keeping it that way—by moving some details down the hierarchy and leaving links behind.

Claude Code’s auto memory keeps its injected layer small in the same way, with Claude maintaining it during the session. Claude doesn’t load all of its auto memory into every session’s context window. It loads only the first 200 lines or 25 KB of . This header serves as an index, which shows Claude what it knows and where to find it.

Dreaming can focus memory on a specific goal

Dreaming can also shape how memory grows. An assistant like Claude Duet, for example, often benefits from having memories that are organized around the person it’s helping, and dreaming can be tuned to build memory in service of a particular goal.

The instructions that guide how memory grows differ by task and tell Claude what information actually matters. For example, one task in the LAB benchmark simulates a company acquisition and provides a set of contracts. The brief is graded on whether it correctly describes the contract terms.

We started with basic instructions for generating the wiki that didn’t tell Claude to use the wiki. This task relied heavily on contract terms. While the wiki was being built, several agents wrote to a shared table of contract terms at the same time (Figure 14, left).

The result was a wiki that was missing key facts. When we graded a brief generated from the wiki, Claude had included only 41 of the 57 facts (72%). When we looked at what had gone wrong, we found that the shared table summarized the contract terms poorly and was missing some of them altogether, because agents had overwritten one another’s work.

The contract terms were the most important part of the wiki, but the instructions didn’t say that. To find better instructions, we ran a loop in which Claude reflected on its failures, proposed a change to the instructions, and rebuilt the wiki. This loop allowed Claude to discover how important it was to follow the contract terms, and it rewrote the instructions for building the wiki accordingly.

Each contract got its own page in the wiki, written by a single agent, which quoted the terms word for word rather than summarizing them into a shared table. When we graded the brief generated from this improved wiki, 100% of the criteria could be met, up from 72%.

Dreaming can fill in gaps a session leaves behind

When Claude writes memory notes, it sees only the context in particular session. Dreaming can search across many sessions to find common patterns or correct common mistakes.

When building the wikis for the LAB benchmark (as an example, see Figure 14), sometimes Claude would link to pages that hadn’t yet been created. A second dreaming pass closed many of these gaps. On one task (Figure 15), dreaming found nine links to a missing page in the wiki and repointed them to an existing page for the same document. It also added three new pages, including an index, to improve the wiki.

Thinking backward, looking forward

There are many open questions about how to design memory systems for agents. One is when Claude should create memory. When Claude works on a task, it can write to a memory store (e.g., a folder, file, or database), capturing salience at the source and making important details immediately available for future turns or sessions. But logging notes in the moment inevitably draws Claude’s attention away from its main task. In contrast, dreaming can push memory creation to the background, but any outputs from dreaming may not be immediately accessible to Claude.

Another question is how to keep memory reliably up to date. Claude can make incorrect predictions or write rules to memory that are wrong from the start. Memory can also drift and become irrelevant as the environment changes. Dreaming is one way to fix these mistakes (Figure 8), but it requires compute. Directing Claude to continuously check its memories might not be practical. It may be important instead to focus dreaming on information that’s likely to change or to carefully tune the cadence of dreaming (e.g., based on how often memories are accessed).

It’s also reasonable to consider transcript search as the foundation of Claude’s memory. Combining representations (e.g., wikis) with search (Figure 10) can sometimes be effective. But Claude needs to use compute to maintain memory representations and make sure they don’t accumulate errors or hallucinations.

Even though Claude’s judgment about salience has improved, no model can really know what will happen in future turns. Dreaming gives Claude an opportunity to look and use compute to organize its memory, correct mistakes, and maintain representations that allow future sessions to access memory more readily. Memory systems will evolve as Claude gets more capable, and we still have a lot to learn about designing Claude’s memory systems.

See our cookbooks for getting started with dreaming and knowledge wikis.

items.title: Greece has its own Pompeii: Thera buried Akrotiri in ash 17th-16th century BCE
items.author: derbOac
items.content:
The earth rumbled for days. Inhabitants of the seafaring Bronze Age settlement ofAkrotiri watched smoke plume from Thera, a long-dormant volcano on what is now the Greek island of Santorini. People gathered their belongings and safely stored the valuables they were forced to leave behind. Then they fled by boat to nearby islands.

When these minor earthquakes and eruptions subsided, residents returned to Akrotiri, collecting materials for reconstruction and beginning the arduous process of repairing the damage. But the ground continued to tremble. As conditions worsened, they made the difficult decision to flee once more, hopeful that their homes would survive the coming devastation.

When Thera erupted again, the explosion was so powerful that it destroyed Akrotiri, burying the settlement (and the island that shared the volcano’s name) in some 200 feet of ash and pumice stone. The timing of the disaster is the subject of intensedebate, but scholars generallydate it to between 1620 and 1530 B.C.E. The event was one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recorded history: Thera released about four times more volcanic material than the infamous Krakatau eruption, which killed upwards of 36,000 people in what is now Indonesia in 1883.

The fallout of the Thera eruption

The ash cloud formed by the Thera eruption completely transformed the island’s lush, humid environment into an arid one. Ash from the volcano was so widespread that it rained down as far as modern-day Egypt and Israel. Layers of sand and pebbles found between archaeological deposits suggest that multipletsunamis also contributed to the destruction.

But the biggest fallout of this cataclysmic event happened when a portion of the volcanic caldera collapsed into the sea a few days after the eruption, forever changing the landscape of Santorini. This plummet into the depths of the Aegean Sea has become the stuff of legends. Some claim that Akrotiri is the lost city of Atlantis, which the Greek philosopher Plato described centuries later, around 360 B.C.E. Most modern scholars, however, agree that Plato created the tale of the sunken island as an allegorical device.

Did you know? The legend of Atlantis

  • In Plato’s telling, Atlantis was home to descendants of the sea god Poseidon, who turned on his progeny after they proved unworthy of his favor. According to the London-based Horniman Museum & Gardens, “The tale warns against the dangers of power and corruption, as well as stressing the importance of goodness.”
  • Plato’s suggests that Atlantis succumbed to “violent earthquakes and floods, and in a single day of misfortune,” the island “disappeared in the depths of the sea.”

Much like the Roman city of Pompeii, which was destroyed when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E., Akrotiri was preserved beneath the ash. “Everything was absolutely annihilated and completely encapsulated on the island,” says Lefteris Zorzos, an archaeologist whose research focuses on the prehistoric landscape of Santorini. This created a rare time capsule that provides an unprecedented look into the daily life of this Middle Bronze Age Cycladic civilization, so called after the Aegean islands where the culture flourished between about 3000 and 1000 B.C.E.

Santorini remained uninhabited for some 700 years. According to the ancient Greek historian Herodotus, Phoenicians started repopulating the island in the ninth century B.C.E. But more than 2,500 years would pass before archaeologists uncovered the ruins of ancient Akrotiri beneath the layers of dirt and ash.

In 1866, miners working in pumice quarries on the island of Therasia, directly west of Thera, discovered a prehistoric building while collecting ash to insulate the Suez Canal. The French School at Athens launched a small excavation of the area in 1870, but a large-scale dig at Akrotiri only commenced nearly a century later, in 1967, under the leadership of archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos.

Marinatos had previously studied the excavated ruins of the Minoan Palace of Knossos in Crete, tracing pumice found on the island, some 74 miles south of Santorini, to the Thera eruption. His research marked the first time that the destruction of Akrotiri was directly linked to the decline of the Minoans, who are often identified as Europe’s first advanced civilization.

Marinatos posited that the earthquakes from Thera were so widespread, they toppled buildings and palaces on Crete. He also suggested that the resulting tsunamis damaged Minoan coastal settlements and halted shipping trade. But this theory is no longer widely accepted, and many historians now believe that the Minoans’ decline can’t be attributed to a single factor. Instead, they point to a combination of environmental changes, declining trade, political instability and conflicts with the ascendant Mycenean civilization.

Preserving an ancient site that was found remarkably intact presented a unique challenge for Marinatos. “When you excavate, you’re destroying a layer, removing the earth that’s keeping it all together,” Zorzos says. “You have to deal with this differently than you would a site that’s not as well preserved.” Before Marinatos could proceed, he had to build a shelter atop the ruins so they wouldn’t crumble when exposed to the elements.

Under the leadership of Marinatos and his successor, Christos Doumas, archaeologists have excavated sites across Akrotiri down to the bedrock, allowing scientists to study the island’s stratigraphy as far back as 6,500 years ago. Zorzos estimates that the ongoing excavations have uncovered only about 10 percent of the settlement. The rest is still preserved beneath layers of ash and sediment.

Surprisingly, researchers have yet to recover the remains of any Akrotiri residents killed by the eruption, suggesting that the majority, if not all, of the settlement’s inhabitants made it out alive after receiving warning of the impending disaster. (Excavations in Turkey have, however, revealed the skeletons of a teenager and a dog believed to be victims of a post-eruption tsunami, testifying to the event’s far reach.) Comparatively, archaeologists excavating the ruins of Pompeii continue to find victims’skeletons (or the cavitiesleft behind by bodies trapped in volcanic ash) nearly 2,000 years after Vesuvius’ eruption.

Researchers can easily understand why Akrotiri’s inhabitants chose to settle in this area. “It has visibility and access to Crete, and it’s strategically connected to the rest of the Cycladic Islands,” says Marianna Nikolaidou, an archaeologist specializing in Aegean culture at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Akrotiri’s location at the crossroads of North Africa, Europe and the Middle East allowed for substantialmaritime trade during the Early Bronze Age (circa 3000 to 2000 B.C.E.). Archaeological evidence suggests that the island community included farmers, fishers and craftspeople.

By the Middle Bronze Age, Crete’s thriving Minoan civilization had left its mark on Akrotiri. The Minoans shared major advancements in architecture with their neighbors, encouraging them to construct multistory buildings adorned with detailed frescoes, paved streets and an impressive drainage system that included indoor plumbing.

In total, archaeologists have identified and researched 35 buildings across Akrotiri. The settlement’s ancient residents “didn’t have access to forests or concrete, and still they are building three- and four-story-high buildings using limited wood, volcanic stones, mud and vegetation,” Zorzos says. “It’s phenomenal to think of how much they were able to achieve without access to modern tools.”

The art and artifacts of Akrotiri

Frescoes in excellent condition adorn the walls of many homes and public buildings in Akrotiri. “Every house had a fresco with a distinct ritual characteristic, and many of them are female-centered,” Nikolaidou says.

Xeste 3, a multistory structure with 14 rooms on each floor, boasts two well-preserved wall paintings. Nikolaidou praises the frescoes’ treatment of their chosen themes, as well as the preparation and finish of the plaster on which they were painted. The first scene depicts three women in a field with crocus flowers and an altar, while the second portrays a different group of women collecting crocuses, which they offer to a goddess attended by a blue monkey and a griffin.

The crocus was a significant symbol in antiquity, with the plant used as a spice, perfume, dye or medicine. “On an island like this with limited resources, crocus must have been a source of economic prosperity, and the fact that it’s associated with women hints to the participation of women in agricultural production and the economic aspects of life, not just the ritual aspects,” Nikolaidou says.

In addition to well-preserved architecture and art, excavations at Akrotiri have unearthed vessels and beads from necklaces. Not much jewelry has been uncovered because inhabitants typically took such valuables with them when they fled. Many of the ceramics depict scenes similar to the wall paintings, providing important clues regarding daily life on the island. Vessels used for transporting oil and wine, and for storing food, feature polychrome scenes of swallows, dolphins and crocuses. Charred remains of barley and fava beans found on the bottom of some of the jugs provide a rare look at the early Mediterranean diet.

One of the most interesting pottery shapes identified at the site is the nippled ewer. “These jugs have a bulbous body, with little pinches that are painted to imitate nipples,” Nikolaidou says. Some of the vessels are even adorned with earrings and necklaces, underscoring the jug’s symbolism as a representation of the female body.

The preservation and future of Akrotiri

Marinatos died in 1974, after an onsite fall during excavations at Akrotiri. Doumas replaced him as director of the archaeological project and has held the position ever since. In 2012, he oversaw the installation of a bioclimatic shelter designed to help preserve the site. The three-acre shelter protects the fragile buildings, with discreet fans extracting the hot air from the surrounding environment. The structure also offers visitors relief from the Mediterranean sun while they explore this settlement frozen in time.

The Akrotiri archaeological site is open to the public most days of the week. Visitors are welcome to explore on their own or with a tour guide who can provide an in-depth explanation of each structure. The nearby Museum of Prehistoric Thera, located about 20 minutes away by car, houses many of the site’s artifacts and is worth a visit.

More than three and a half millennia after Thera’s eruption, the Santorini community is working with the Archaeological Society at Athens to continue to preserve and fund the site. In 2027, Santorini will celebrate the 60th anniversary of the official start of excavations—an occasion that will be marked with exhibitions, educational programs and other events.

Akrotiri’s ruins have revealed the long-overlooked story of a cosmopolitan society connected to the outside world. The settlement’s inhabitants were voyagers and artisans with sophisticated and clearly defined social stratification, but they also had a strong sense of collectivity and community that survives on Santorini today. “It’s one of the most important archaeological sites in the world,” Zorzos says. “It provides a window into life in the prehistoric Aegean like we’ve never seen before.”
